full_judgment:
6. Mr. Karim's contention is that, his client is not responsible for the missing of the ballot papers. In the absence of entire set of ballot papers, it is not possible or proper for the Tribunal to act on incomplete and insufficient ballots. According to him, this missing of ballot papers has taken place after the election. Post election fact cannot relate back to nullify the anterior fact of election. The tribunal ought not to have taken note of incomplete ballot papers, but proceeded on the presumption of regularity of official acts under S. 114(c) of the Evidence Act. Mr. Karim contends that there is every possibility that, had all the ballot papers been produced, the number of invalid votes in favour of respondent Nani Chandra might have been greater and the margin of difference in favour of the appellant increased instead of decreasing. 

 7. Mr. B.N. Chowdhury for the respondent Nani Chandra argues, that each ballot paper is an independent piece of evidence, and therefore rightly admitted into evidence and if from the ballot papers produced, a margin of difference decisive against the appellant could be spelt out it could be done in law. He further submits that presumption of regularity has been amply rebutted, when the tribunal found that quite a large number of invalid votes were cast in favour of the appellant. 

 8. The learned Attorney-General-referring to Rule Nos. 40, 42, 44 and 81 submits ballot papers are no doubt; good pieces of-evidence in an election dispute and the tribunal is to proceed on the presumption of regularity of official business under S. 114(c) of the Evidence Act. But this presumption is tribunal. It is for the tribunal to say, whether the evidence produced is sufficient to rebut the presumption under S. 144(e) of the Evidence Act. The qua-tum of evidence necessary to rebut the presumption is a question more of fact than law. 

 11. A reference to the rules indicates that ballot papers are the principal pieces of evidence for adjudicating the validity of election, both for the purpose of declaration and trial. Rules also show that ballot papers in aggregate will decide the result of election, nonetheless each ballot paper is separate and distinct, and it stands or falls on its own merit. Aggregate valid ballot papers will no doubt decide the result of election, but then the aggregate cannot be treated a unity. This being the legal position of ballot papers, non-production of some will not render the ballot papers produced inadmissible. Mr. Karim's contention that non-production of all ballot papers has rendered the papers produced inadmissible cannot be sustained. That does not however support the submission of Mr. Chowdhury that the papers produced will rebut the presumption of regularity, and for the non-produced papers the said presumption will subsist. This is approbation and reprobation and cannot be accepted. 

 12. We find that the question turns upon the sufficiency of evidence. It is a question of fact and will be determined on the facts of each case, and no hard and, fast rule can be prescribed. If the ballot papers produced are sufficient to adjudicate the disputed claims between the rival candidates, the Tribunal can proceed to decide the issue between the parties. But when the papers produced are small and the papers not produced large and adjudication is not possible, the Tribunal will not act upon ballot papers produced; but then the ground will not be one of admissibility but of adequacy of evidence. In the total absence of evidence of ballot papers, when none of the parties is responsible for their non-production the Tribunal may act on the resumption of regularity of official act under S. 114(c) of the Evidence Act. But this presumption of regularity is a rebuttable one. What should be the quantum of evidence to rebut this presumption will depend upon the facts of each case.
